title: The bat and the ball
prompt: A bat and a ball cost $1.10 in total. The bat costs $1.00 more than the ball. How much does the ball cost?
why: If the ball is x, the bat is x + 1.00, so 2x + 1.00 = 1.10 and x = 0.05. The fast answer of 10 cents makes the bat only 90 cents more expensive.

title: Doubling lily pads
prompt: A patch of lily pads doubles in size every day. It covers the whole lake on day 48. On which day did it cover half the lake?
why: Doubling means the day before full coverage it was exactly half. Exponential growth is not linear: halving the time does not halve the size.

title: Machines and widgets
prompt: 5 machines make 5 widgets in 5 minutes. How long do 100 machines take to make 100 widgets?
why: Each machine makes one widget in 5 minutes. 100 machines working in parallel make 100 widgets in the same 5 minutes.

title: The overtake
prompt: In a race you overtake the runner in second place. What place are you in now?
why: You take the place of the runner you passed. The person in first is still ahead of you.

title: Knights and knaves
prompt: Knights always tell the truth and knaves always lie. A says: "We are both knaves." What are A and B?
options: A is a knight, B is a knave
A is a knave, B is a knight
why: A knight could never say he is a knave, so A is a knave and his statement is false. "Both knaves" being false while A is a knave means B must be a knight.

title: Three switches, one bulb
prompt: Three switches outside a closed room control one bulb inside. You may flip switches as you like, then enter the room. What is the minimum number of times you must enter the room to know which switch controls the bulb?
options: It cannot be known for certain
why: Turn switch 1 on for ten minutes, turn it off, turn switch 2 on, then go in. Lit: switch 2. Off but warm: switch 1. Off and cold: switch 3. The bulb's heat is a second bit of information.

title: The heavier ball
prompt: You have 9 identical-looking balls. One is slightly heavier. With a balance scale, what is the minimum number of weighings that guarantees finding it?
why: Each weighing has three outcomes (left, right, balanced), so split into three groups of 3. One weighing finds the heavy group, the second finds the ball. 3^2 = 9.

title: Three doors
prompt: A prize is behind one of three doors. You pick door 1. The host, who knows where the prize is, opens door 3 to show it is empty and offers you door 2. If you switch, what is your chance of winning?
why: Your first pick is right 1/3 of the time. The other 2/3 of the time the prize is behind one of the other doors, and the host has just shown you which one. Switching wins exactly when your first pick was wrong.

title: Counting handshakes
prompt: At a meeting every pair of people shook hands exactly once. There were 66 handshakes. How many people were there?
why: n people make n(n - 1)/2 handshakes. 12 × 11 / 2 = 66. Same formula as counting pairs in a nested loop where j starts after i.

title: Clock hands
prompt: What is the angle between the hour hand and the minute hand at 3:15?
why: The minute hand is at 90°. The hour hand moves 0.5° per minute, so at 3:15 it sits at 90° + 7.5° = 97.5°. The hands are 7.5° apart, not overlapping.

title: Socks in the dark
prompt: A drawer holds 10 black socks and 10 white socks. In the dark, how many socks must you pull out to guarantee two black socks?
why: Worst case you pull all 10 white socks first. Two more are then guaranteed to be black: 12. Guaranteeing any matching pair would only need 3.

title: Overlapping skills
prompt: In a team of 30 developers, 18 know Python, 15 know JavaScript and 4 know neither. How many know both?
why: 26 people know at least one. Inclusion-exclusion: 18 + 15 - both = 26, so both = 7.

title: Shared birthdays
prompt: What is the smallest group size for a better than 50% chance that two people share a birthday (365 equally likely days)?
why: With 23 people there are 253 pairs, and the chance that all birthdays differ drops just below 50%. This is why hash collisions arrive much sooner than intuition says.

title: The fly between two trains
prompt: Two trains 100 km apart drive toward each other at 50 km/h each. A fly flies at 75 km/h from one train to the other and back until the trains meet. How far does the fly travel in total?
why: The trains close at 100 km/h, so they meet after 1 hour. The fly flies for that hour at 75 km/h. No infinite series needed.

title: Average speed
prompt: You drive 60 km at 30 km/h, then 60 km at 90 km/h. What was your average speed for the whole trip?
why: Time is 2 h + 2/3 h = 8/3 h for 120 km, so 45 km/h. Averaging the two speeds ignores that you spent far longer at the slow one.

title: Searching a sorted list
prompt: A sorted array holds 1,000,000 elements. At most how many comparisons does binary search need to find an element or prove it is absent?
why: Each comparison halves the range. 2^20 = 1,048,576, which is just over a million, so 20 comparisons suffice.

title: Two children
prompt: A family has two children. You learn that at least one of them is a boy. What is the probability that both are boys?
why: Equally likely families are BB, BG, GB, GG. "At least one boy" removes GG, leaving three cases, one of which is BB.

title: Burning ropes
prompt: Two ropes each take exactly 60 minutes to burn, but they burn unevenly. How can you measure exactly 45 minutes?
options: Cut each rope at three quarters of its length
Light rope A at both ends and rope B at one end; when A finishes, light B's other end
Light both ropes at both ends at the same time
It cannot be done because the ropes burn unevenly
why: A burning from both ends finishes in 30 minutes whatever its shape. At that moment B has 30 minutes left; lighting its other end halves that to 15. 30 + 15 = 45. Cutting fails because the burn rate is uneven.

title: The poisoned bottle
prompt: One of 1,000 bottles is poisoned. A test strip shows positive a day after touching any amount of poison, and you only have time for one round of testing. What is the minimum number of strips that identifies the bottle?
why: Number the bottles in binary. Strip k tests every bottle whose bit k is 1. The positive strips spell out the poisoned bottle's number. 2^10 = 1,024 ≥ 1,000.

title: 100 lockers
prompt: 100 closed lockers. Student 1 toggles every locker, student 2 toggles every 2nd, student 3 every 3rd, and so on up to student 100. How many lockers end up open?
why: A locker is toggled once per divisor. Only perfect squares have an odd number of divisors, so lockers 1, 4, 9 ... 100 stay open: 10 of them.

title: Zeros at the end
prompt: How many zeros are at the end of 100! (100 factorial)?
why: Each trailing zero needs a factor of 5 (twos are plentiful). Multiples of 5 give 20, multiples of 25 give 4 more: 24.

title: Two guards, two doors
prompt: One door leads to freedom, the other to a dungeon. One guard always lies and one always tells the truth, but you don't know which is which. You may ask one guard one question. What works?
options: Ask either guard: "Are you the truthful one?"
Ask either guard: "Which door would the other guard say leads to freedom?" and take the other door
Ask either guard: "Which door leads to freedom?" and take that door
why: The question routes through both guards, so the answer always contains exactly one lie and always points to the dungeon. Take the opposite door.

title: Counting recursive calls
prompt: f(n) returns 1 when n == 0 and otherwise returns f(n - 1) + f(n - 1). How many calls to f happen in total when you call f(10)?
why: The calls form a full binary tree of depth 10: 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 1,024 = 2^11 - 1 = 2,047. Calling f(n - 1) once and doubling it would make 11.

title: Two heads in a row
prompt: You flip a fair coin until you get two heads in a row. On average, how many flips does that take?
why: Let E be the expected flips from the start. Tails sends you back (cost 1 + E), heads then tails sends you back (cost 2 + E), heads heads finishes in 2. E = ½(1 + E) + ¼(2 + E) + ¼·2 gives E = 6.

title: Two eggs, 100 floors
prompt: You have 2 identical eggs and a 100-floor building. An egg breaks if dropped from floor F or higher. What is the minimum number of drops that guarantees finding F in the worst case?
why: Drop the first egg from floors 14, 27, 39 ... shrinking the gap by one each time so the worst case stays constant. You need k with k(k + 1)/2 ≥ 100: k = 14.

title: Ali and Sara
prompt: Ali is twice as old as Sara was when Ali was as old as Sara is now. Ali is 24. How old is Sara?
why: The age gap is 24 - S. When Ali was S, Sara was S - (24 - S) = 2S - 24. So 24 = 2(2S - 24), giving S = 18. Check: six years ago Ali was 18 and Sara was 12, and 24 = 2 × 12.

title: The night bridge
prompt: Four people must cross a bridge at night with one torch. At most two cross at a time, at the slower person's pace, and the torch must be carried back. They take 1, 2, 5 and 10 minutes. What is the fastest total time?
why: 1 and 2 cross (2), 1 returns (1), 5 and 10 cross together (10), 2 returns (2), 1 and 2 cross (2): 17. Escorting everyone with the 1-minute walker gives 19 because the two slowest pay separately.
